generalfeedback.text: Record cost as well as quality — Friday's tool needs no training or ground truth, and the comparison is meaningless without that.

answer.text: Friday's tool needs no training, no line-fixing, and no examples, so comparing quality without comparing cost misses half the question.

feedback.text: Correct. The honest Week 5 assessment needs both figures.

answer.text: Because the time spent is part of the mark for the Transcription Assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It feeds the report's argument, not a time-based mark.

answer.text: Because Transkribus bills credits by the hour and you must report usage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credits are consumed by training runs, and that is not why the time is recorded.

answer.text: Because slower training indicates a mismatched base model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The timing being recorded is your effort, not the machine's.

name.text: 23 Content: Why the Small Specialist Usually Wins

questiontext.text:
Why the Small Specialist Usually Wins

Worth understanding before Friday, because the result goes against instinct.

The general AI models are enormous, trained on staggering amounts of material. Your model is tiny and learned from a few dozen lines of one scribe. Instinct says the big one should win.

On historical manuscripts it usually does not, and the gap is huge. On a medieval Latin test set, a model tuned for medieval Latin got 14.6% of characters wrong, while a large commercial system scored 84.7% on identical pages (Mattingly et al., 2024). On historical English, GPT-4o got 52.23% wrong; on historical German, 77.42% (AlKendi et al., 2024).

The same models are superb on modern handwriting. GPT-4o gets 1.39% wrong on a modern English test set — as good as purpose-built tools (AlKendi et al., 2024).

Material Model Wrong
Modern English GPT-4o 1.39%
Historical English GPT-4o 52.23%
Historical German GPT-4o 77.42%
Medieval Latin Tuned specialist 14.6%
Medieval Latin Large general model 84.7%

This is the specialization gap. The specialists are far smaller and win because they have actually been shown scribal handwriting, odd short forms, joined letters, and irregular layouts (Mattingly et al., 2024). The general models have seen the internet, and the internet contains very little Byzantine Greek minuscule.

Size does not substitute for having seen the material. Friday you check this on your own manuscript.

Vocabulary. Benchmark — a standard test set used to compare tools fairly. General-purpose model — one trained on everything rather than for one job.

Takeaway: General models are excellent on modern handwriting and catastrophic on historical scripts — scale does not substitute for exposure to the material.

name.text: 23 Question: Why the Small Specialist Usually Wins

questiontext.text: GPT-4o gets 1.39% wrong on modern English handwriting and 52.23% on historical English. What does the gap show?

generalfeedback.text: General models are excellent on modern handwriting and catastrophic on historical scripts — scale does not substitute for exposure to the material.

answer.text: Sheer size does not substitute for having been shown the actual material — the internet holds very little old handwriting.

feedback.text: Correct. Same model, same language; only the century changed.

answer.text: That historical English is a fundamentally harder language than modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the same language. What differs is how well represented the handwriting is.

answer.text: That the historical test set was too small to give a reliable figure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing suggests that, and the pattern repeats across several datasets and models.

answer.text: That the model needs a larger image resolution for historical documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution is not what accounts for a fortyfold difference.

name.text: 24 Content: More Steps Can Make It Worse

questiontext.text:
More Steps Can Make It Worse

A related finding, worth knowing before Friday because it will shape what you try.

The instinct when assembling a workflow is that more helpers must help: a reading program, then an AI to tidy its mistakes, maybe a lookup step to supply background knowledge. Each addition fixes something real.

In practice it backfires. A plain workflow — one specialist reading program feeding one translator — beats versions with extra AI steps bolted on. The extra generative steps introduce their own errors, and those errors then travel downstream unchecked (Mattingly et al., 2024).

Workflow Extra pieces Result
Plain None Best
Plus background lookup One Worse
Plus AI tidying of the reading One Worse
Both Two Worst

The mechanism is simple. Every generative step can break things as well as fix them, and something broken late in the chain has nothing after it to catch the problem. An AI tidying up reading output cannot see the picture. It corrects toward whatever sounds most likely — which means it will "fix" a correct but unusual reading into a wrong but ordinary one. In manuscripts, the unusual readings are frequently the interesting ones.

So, for Friday: do not try to improve today's output by passing it through an AI to clean up. That is exactly the setup the evidence says makes things worse, and you would be degrading your text while feeling you had improved it.

Vocabulary. Pipeline — a chain of processing steps, each feeding the next. Error propagation — a mistake made early travelling onward unnoticed.

Takeaway: Adding LLM post-correction to OCR degrades quality — it corrects toward plausibility, and unusual readings are the interesting ones.

name.text: 24 Question: More Steps Can Make It Worse

questiontext.text: Why does adding an AI step to tidy up reading output make the result worse rather than better?

generalfeedback.text: Adding LLM post-correction to OCR degrades quality — it corrects toward plausibility, and unusual readings are the interesting ones.

answer.text: The tidying step cannot see the picture, so it corrects toward whatever sounds likely — and unusual readings are often the interesting ones.

feedback.text: Correct. Anything broken late in the chain has nothing after it to catch the problem.

answer.text: Because the extra step doubles the processing time for no gain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The cost is quality, not time.

answer.text: Because the two programs use incompatible character encodings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Encoding is not the issue — the issue is correcting toward plausibility without seeing the source.

answer.text: Because the tidying step overwrites the raw output, so nothing can be measured.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You can keep both. The finding is that the tidied text is genuinely worse.

name.text: 25 Content: Checklist Before You Leave

questiontext.text:
Checklist Before You Leave

Check each one.

  • Manuscript imported into Transkribus by web address.
  • Line-finding run on every leaf you are using.
  • Every line found; no merges or splits left.
  • Strips checked to include the high accents.
  • Your transcription attached to the right lines, spot-checked.
  • Starting model chosen, with the reason written down.
  • Model trained, with a representative set of lines held back.
  • Score recorded.
  • Model run on at least one untyped leaf.
  • Output read line by line, zoomed in.
  • Mistakes sorted in logs/htr-errors-w4.md.
  • Raw output committed on its own, with the labels.
  • Raw output tagged.
  • ALTO or PAGE export committed.
  • Coordinates checked against your Lesson 3.3 measured lines.
  • Time spent recorded.

If your score is worse than 15%, do not start correcting. The output is not worth the effort. Diagnose instead, in the order from section 14: line-finding, then alignment, then how much training material, then the starting model.

Vocabulary. Spot-check — verifying a few samples rather than everything. Diagnose — work out the cause before attempting a fix.

Takeaway: If validation CER exceeds 15%, diagnose rather than correct — check layout, then alignment, then data volume, then base model.

name.text: 25 Question: Checklist Before You Leave

questiontext.text: In what order should you diagnose a model that scored worse than 15%?

generalfeedback.text: If validation CER exceeds 15%, diagnose rather than correct — check layout, then alignment, then data volume, then base model.

answer.text: Line-finding, then alignment, then how much training material, then the starting model.

feedback.text: Correct. Most first models are fixable, and the order runs from the most likely cause to the least.

answer.text: Starting model, then training passes, then image resolution, then alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The starting model is checked last, not first — line-finding faults are far more common.

answer.text: Retrain immediately with more passes before investigating anything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. More passes will not fix bad strips or mismatched text, and it spends shared credits.

answer.text: Correct the output first, then retrain on the corrections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Above 15% the output is not worth correcting — that is the whole point of the threshold.

name.text: 26 Content: Things That Go Wrong Today

questiontext.text:
Things That Go Wrong Today

The failures that keep happening, and what they mean.

Symptom Likely cause What to check
Import fails Address not reachable publicly curl from outside your network
Some lines not found Faint ink; settings Look, then fix by hand
No accents at all in the output Strips cutting them off Look at the extracted strips
Fluent nonsense Text attached one line out Spot-check picture against words
Score far worse than expected Starting model wrong for the script Confirm script and date
Good on one leaf, bad on another Different layouts Test each layout separately
Training improves, held-back lines worsen Memorizing Stop at the low point
Words glued together Words run together on the page Expected; note it for Week 5
Short forms spelled out Starting model learned tidy text Pick a diplomatic starting model

Rows three and four are today's signature failures, and both are invisible in the output itself. Missing accents look like the program being weak at Greek rather than a strip problem. Text attached one line out reads perfectly and simply belongs somewhere else.

The remedy for both is the same, and it is worth keeping as a general rule: when output is wrong in a way you cannot explain, go and look at what the program actually saw. The extracted strip is the truth about the input, and nearly every baffling failure is visible there.

Vocabulary. Symptom — what you observe going wrong. Cause — the underlying fault, often several steps earlier.

Takeaway: When output is inexplicably wrong, look at the extracted line image — that is what the model actually saw.

name.text: 26 Question: Things That Go Wrong Today

questiontext.text: The output is fluent and reads coherently, but it does not match the page. What is the likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: When output is inexplicably wrong, look at the extracted line image — that is what the model actually saw.

answer.text: Your transcription was attached one line out, so the model learned each line's picture with the next line's words.

feedback.text: Correct. The text is internally coherent and simply belongs somewhere else — spot-check picture against words to confirm.

answer.text: The strips were cut too tightly, removing the accents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That produces text missing its accents, not coherent text belonging elsewhere.

answer.text: The base model was trained on tidied text and is spelling short forms out.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That shows as expanded abbreviations, not as wholesale displacement.

answer.text: The model overfitted and is reproducing memorized training lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Memorized lines would match the page they came from. Here the pairing itself is wrong.

name.text: 27 Content: Writing Down What You Did

questiontext.text:
Writing Down What You Did

Your Week 5 report needs an account of today's work. Writing it now is far easier than reconstructing it later.

Record in logs/htr-method-w4.md:

  • Which platform, and which version.
  • Which model you started from, what it was trained on, how it performs.
  • Your own material: which leaves, how many lines, how produced.
  • What line-fixing was needed, and of what kind.
  • Whether you changed the line-finding settings, and to what.
  • How you trained: how many lines held back, how many passes, when you stopped.
  • The score, and what it was measured on.
  • Which leaves you then ran the model over.
  • The kinds of mistake you saw, with counts.
  • Time spent at each stage.

This is a methods section. Its job is to let a reader — or you in December — see what was done and judge whether the results mean what they seem to. A score of 6.2% means nothing without knowing the starting model, how much material, and what was in the held-back set.

It also protects you. If your Week 5 results are surprising, this record is what lets you work out why. Without it, a strange number is simply strange, and your only option is doing the work again.

Commit it with a docs: prefix.

Vocabulary. Methods section — the part of a report saying exactly what was done. Provenance — the documented history of how something was made.

Takeaway: A CER figure is uninterpretable without its base model, training volume, and validation set — record the methodology today.

name.text: 27 Question: Writing Down What You Did

questiontext.text: Why is a score of 6.2% meaningless on its own?

generalfeedback.text: A CER figure is uninterpretable without its base model, training volume, and validation set — record the methodology today.

answer.text: Without the starting model, the amount of training material, and what was in the held-back set, nobody can tell what it measures.

feedback.text: Correct. Record it now — if Week 5's results surprise you, this is what lets you work out why.

answer.text: Because scores must always be reported alongside a word-level figure as well.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A word-level figure helps, but it is not what makes the character figure interpretable.

answer.text: Because 6.2% is within the margin of error for any small test set.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing in the lesson suggests that. The problem is missing context, not statistical noise.

answer.text: Because scores are only comparable between students using the same manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are not comparable between manuscripts, but that is not why the methodology is recorded.

name.text: 28 Content: Preparing for Friday

questiontext.text:
Preparing for Friday

Friday is remote, and it puts the same passage through a general AI model.

Have all of this available from wherever you will be:

  • Your repository, pushed.
  • Yesterday's transcription, tagged.
  • Today's raw output, tagged.
  • Today's sorted mistakes and methods notes.
  • Your images, reachable from outside your network.
  • A working Greek keyboard on the machine you will use.
  • Access to an AI model that accepts pictures.

Friday's comparison is three-way: your typing, today's specialist model, and Friday's general model, all on the same lines. Having all three saved under tags is what makes that comparison exact rather than roughly right.

Set your expectation now, so the result is a measurement rather than a shock. Going by the published figures in section 23, Friday's output will probably be much worse than today's on historical Greek. It will also arrive in minutes instead of a whole session. Week 5 needs you to hold both of those facts at once.

Check your setup today, following Lesson 4.1 section 23. Every item takes two minutes now and none of them takes two minutes on Friday morning.

Vocabulary. Three-way comparison — measuring three versions of the same passage against each other. Tag — a permanent name on one saved version.

Takeaway: Tag all three states so Friday's three-way comparison is exact, and expect the general model to be much worse and much faster.

name.text: 28 Question: Preparing for Friday

questiontext.text: Why must all three versions be saved under tags before Friday?

generalfeedback.text: Tag all three states so Friday's three-way comparison is exact, and expect the general model to be much worse and much faster.

answer.text: Friday compares your typing, today's model, and the general AI on the same lines, and tags make that comparison exact rather than approximate.

feedback.text: Correct. A tag is a permanent name for one particular version, retrievable from anywhere.

answer.text: Because tagged versions are the only ones that can be pushed from off campus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any commit can be pushed. Tags do need pushing explicitly, which is a separate trap.

answer.text: Because the AI model reads the tags to know which version to compare against.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It reads a picture. The tags are for you and for Week 5.

answer.text: Because untagged work is not eligible for the Transcription Assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The requirement is methodological — exact retrieval of the state that was measured.

name.text: 29 Content: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text:
What Good Work Looks Like Here

"Trained a model" and "trained a model well" are different achievements.

An acceptable result is a trained model with a recorded score and output you have looked at.

Good work also:

  • Fixes the line-finding thoroughly, including the strips around accents.
  • Checks that text is attached to the right lines instead of assuming it.
  • Chooses a starting model deliberately and says why.
  • Holds back a representative set of lines, not a convenient one.
  • Sorts mistakes into kinds rather than just counting them.
  • Tells line-finding failures apart from reading failures.
  • Records cost — time and effort — alongside quality.
  • Commits raw output separately from corrections, fully labelled.
  • Says what the model does badly, and offers a reason.

That last one is what makes this scholarship rather than button-pushing. "6% wrong, and it drops breathings on one particular letter, fails on this scribe's short form for kai, and falls apart on the glossed leaf" is far more useful than "6% wrong" — because it tells you what to fix, what to check by hand, and what to say about whether this method suits this manuscript.

Vocabulary. Qualitative — concerning the kind of thing, not the amount. Hypothesis — a proposed explanation you can go on to test.

Takeaway: Reporting what the model gets wrong and why is the scholarly contribution; the CER number alone is tool operation.

name.text: 29 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What turns today's work from button-pushing into scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Reporting *what* the model gets wrong and why is the scholarly contribution; the CER number alone is tool operation.

answer.text: Saying what the model gets wrong and why — which letterform, which short form, which kind of page.

feedback.text: Correct. That tells you what to fix, what to check by hand, and whether the method suits this manuscript. A bare score does none of it.

answer.text: Reaching a score below 5%, which is the threshold for a publishable model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such threshold, and a low score can conceal serious damage.

answer.text: Training several models and reporting the best score achieved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reporting only the best run hides more than it shows.

answer.text: Using the largest available base model, to rule out undertraining.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Larger is not better here — matched is better.

name.text: 30 Content: Synthesis: An Instrument with Edges

questiontext.text:
Synthesis: An Instrument with Edges

What today established about the machine step.

A specialized reading model is an instrument with edges. It reads ink and produces letters, and it is competent exactly as far as its examples went. Inside that boundary, on handwriting it has seen, it is fast, cheap, consistent, and — because it barely models language — inclined to fail loudly rather than to invent (Puigcerver, 2017; AlKendi et al., 2024).

How well it works depends on things you control. The line-finding has to be fixed, because the reading step only ever sees what line-finding produced, and chopped strips delete Greek accents before the model lays eyes on them (Perdiki & Konstantinidou, 2023). Your text must be attached to the right lines. The starting model must match the script. And you must start from an existing model, because that alone was the difference between 17% and 4% on identical material (Perdiki & Konstantinidou, 2023).

Judging it takes more than a number. A score holds only for pages laid out like the ones it was tested on, treats every difference as equal, and can look excellent while the model quietly modernizes away the very fidelity your edition exists to preserve (Levchenko, 2024).

Friday tests the opposite kind of instrument: no edges, trained on everything, able to draw on what language usually does — and therefore able to produce fluent text that is not on the page. Comparing the two is the point of the week.

For Friday. Remote. Bring the seven items in section 28, with all three versions tagged.

Vocabulary. Bounded — limited to a defined range of material. Fluent — reading smoothly, which is not the same as being correct.

Takeaway: An HTR model reads ink within the bounds of its training and fails conspicuously; Friday's instrument reads expectation too, and fails fluently.

References

AlKendi, W., Gechter, F., Heyberger, L., & Guyeux, C. (2024). Advancements and challenges in handwritten text recognition: A comprehensive survey. Journal of Imaging.

eScriptorium/Kraken. (2024). eScriptorium platform documentation. https://escriptorium.eu/about

Geelhaar, T. (2022). Carolingian minuscule model CMM 9th–11th c. Transkribus Model. https://www.transkribus.org/models/latin-carolingian-minuscule

Levchenko, M. A. (2024). Evaluating LLMs for historical document OCR: A methodological framework for digital humanities.

Li, M., Lv, T., Chen, J., Cui, L., Lu, Y., Florencio, D., Zhang, C., Li, Z., & Wei, F. (2023). TrOCR: Transformer-based optical character recognition with pre-trained models. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 37(11), 13094–13102.

Mattingly, W. J. B., et al. (2024). When simpler is better: Evaluating translation pipelines for medieval Latin manuscripts.

Perdiki, E., & Konstantinidou, M. (2023). Preparing big manuscript data for hierarchical clustering with minimal HTR training. Journal of Data Mining & Digital Humanities. https://jdmdh.episciences.org/12664/pdf

Puigcerver, J. (2017). PyLaia: A deep learning toolkit for handwritten document analysis. https://github.com/jpuigcerver/PyLaia

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: An Instrument with Edges

questiontext.text: What does it mean to call a trained reading model "an instrument with edges"?

generalfeedback.text: An HTR model reads ink within the bounds of its training and fails conspicuously; Friday's instrument reads expectation too, and fails fluently.

answer.text: It reads ink and produces letters, and its competence extends exactly as far as its examples went — no further, and it does not pretend otherwise.

feedback.text: Correct. Inside that boundary it is fast, cheap, consistent, and inclined to fail loudly rather than to invent.

answer.text: It works only on rectangular pages with clearly ruled margins.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The edges are the limits of its training, not a physical constraint on the page.

answer.text: It has a fixed maximum accuracy that no amount of training can exceed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy improves with better data. The boundary is about what material it can handle.

answer.text: It must be retrained from scratch whenever the manuscript changes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You fine-tune it further — starting from scratch is precisely what you should never do.
